From Hands-On Support to Multi-Site IT Leadership

Over more than a decade in IT, my work has progressed from direct technical support and endpoint troubleshooting into infrastructure, enterprise applications, vendor coordination, security, and multi-site technology leadership.
I lead day-to-day technology operations across seven hotels and additional business assets and corporate partners, supporting both front-of-house and back-of-house environments.

The role spans networks, endpoints, Microsoft services, identity, property-management systems, point-of-sale platforms, A/V, telecommunications, vendor coordination, project work, and operational escalations.

Because hospitality operates around the clock, technical decisions have to account for business continuity, guest impact, employee productivity, revenue systems, security, and the ability to recover quickly when something fails.
The work moves constantly between immediate support, escalation, infrastructure, project coordination, security, and longer-term operational improvement.

Hospitality IT crosses traditional enterprise systems and property-specific technology. A workstation problem may depend on identity, DNS, networking, a hosted application, a vendor-managed service, or an upstream connectivity issue.
My role is often to identify those dependencies quickly enough to determine ownership, impact, and the safest path to restoration.
Much of the role is about improving the environment around support, not just solving isolated technical incidents.
My security focus has grown directly from operating environments where access, identity, endpoints, availability, and business continuity cannot be separated from one another.
Modern IT environments depend on managed providers, software vendors, telecommunications carriers, installers, property-system partners, and other external teams.

My responsibility does not end when an issue technically belongs to another provider. I still need to establish impact, provide useful evidence, coordinate the correct parties, track ownership, communicate with the operation, and move the issue toward resolution.
That requires technical depth to challenge assumptions, operational awareness to prioritize correctly, and communication strong enough to keep multiple groups aligned.

The common thread through my career has been increasing ownership: first understanding individual technical problems, then systems and dependencies, and eventually the broader operation around those systems.

Infrastructure I Can Operate, Break, and Rebuild
The lab gives me an environment where storage, networking, applications, Linux, containers, and media services all depend on one another.

It has evolved through hardware changes, storage migrations, application failures, permission issues, media-library problems, networking troubleshooting, and experiments with different self-hosted services.

The value of the platform is not any single application. It is the experience of running infrastructure where failures must be diagnosed across layers and where recovery matters as much as deployment.
Real services create real dependencies. That makes the platform useful for learning because storage, permissions, networking, containers, applications, and recovery all matter.
Storage is the foundation of the lab. Media services, containers, application data, configuration, and long-term files all depend on the underlying ZFS environment.
Working with ZFS has required understanding more than disk capacity. Pools, datasets, permissions, caching, snapshots, and workload behavior all affect how the system operates.

One of the useful lessons has been learning that high memory consumption is not automatically a problem. ZFS ARC uses available memory aggressively for caching, so system health has to be evaluated in context rather than by looking at a single utilization number.

A practical workflow for responding to repeated unauthorized MFA prompts, including containment, authentication review, recovery, and lessons learned.
Repeated MFA prompts that a user did not initiate should be treated as a potential identity-security incident, not simply an annoying authentication problem.

A user reports receiving repeated MFA prompts even though they are not actively signing in. The immediate temptation may be to troubleshoot the authenticator application or assume the prompts are accidental.
But an unexpected MFA request may indicate that someone is attempting to authenticate using the user's identity and has reached the MFA stage of the sign-in process.
At that point, the issue should be treated as a potential identity-security incident rather than routine authentication support.
The early objective is to establish whether the activity is legitimate, reduce the chance of continued access, and preserve enough evidence to understand what happened.
The goal is to reconstruct what the identity was doing rather than relying only on the user's memory of the prompts.
Security Still Has to Support the User
In an operational environment, an account may be tied to email, property systems, collaboration tools, file access, and other services the user needs to perform their job.
That does not mean containment should be delayed. It means the response should include communication, ownership, recovery planning, and an understanding of what business processes may be affected.
The objective is not simply to lock an account. It is to reduce risk, understand what happened, and safely return the user to normal operation.
An MFA Prompt Can Be an Incident Signal

MFA is an important control, but an unexpected prompt can also become a useful security signal. Authentication requests the user did not initiate should trigger validation, investigation, and a response proportional to the evidence.
